newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Australia telecom watchdog says has bite.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Australia telecom watchdog says has bite.

text.p: Anti-monoplies body the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said it was confident that it had the resources and the expertise to police the soon-to-be deregulated telecommunications market.

Rod Shogren, who has been nominated telecommunications commissioner for the ACCC, said the watchdog had set up a telecommunications unit and would employ people with special skills and experience in the industry.
"We are confident that we will be able to do our job properly," Shogren told Reuters in a telephone interview.
However concerns have been raised by some telecoms groups, who feel the ACCC has not got the experience in telecoms to deal with the industry issues.

"We are concerned that the ACCC might not have the resources or the skills and it might not have the will possibly to administer the act in the way we believe it needs to be done," said Brian Perkins of telecoms lobby group Span.
Perkins said if the ACCC fails in policing the industry properly the sector could fall back into a duopoly.
ACCC takes over from Austel as telecoms watchdog from July 1, when the sector becomes fully open to competition.
Funding for the ACCC has been boosted to assume its extra responsibilities in the telecoms sector. The commission monitors anti-competitor behaviour across all industries in Australia.
However, Perkins said a new telecommunications bill looked robust enough to deal with anti-competitive behaviour and at the same time promote increased competition.

Deregulation puts the Australian government in a delicate situation as it tries to nurture increased telecoms competition while at the same time it has to extract maximum value from its proposed sell-off of a third of Telstra Corp Ltd.

ACCC's Shogren said the new era of deregulation will sweep away current preferred regulatory treatment for Optus Communications, which was formed in 1992 as the only competitor to former telephone monoploy Telstra in the fixed line business.

"The industry has been used to a well-defined regulatory framework in the sense that Optus was given a specifically preferred position as a duopolist and we are moving away from that to a position where everyone is treated equally," Shogren said.
Shogren, a former official at the Australian treasury in Canberra, said Optus was given preferential treatment in order to foster competition with Telstra.
"It is quite a big change and people will have to get used to the idea that they are now treated as part of the general competition law of the country," Shogren said.
On Wednesday the ACCC recommended a 35-percent reduction for interconnect fees with the Telstra network, which is the country's main telephone network.
This is seen by industry players as one of the first steps to encouraging competition in Australia's A$25 billion telecommunications market.
The ACCC will have the power to impose fines of A$10 million for anti-competitive behaviour, plus A$1 million a day for breaches if the commission's rules are upheld in court.

However, Shogren said as telecommunications commissioner he would have limited power in determining the outcome of any potential shake-up in Australia's loss making pay television industry, which both Optus and Telstra are involved in.

Telstra and Optus have both invested heavily in Australia's pay TV sector, which has lost investors almost A$2 billion since 1993. Rationalisation in the loss-making pay-TV sector has long been tipped to curtail further losses.
